title: Covered with truth
hookLine: a family asks a dying man, do you know me? then an accused man grips a red-hot axe, covered with truth
carry: satya: truth stands on what is real
last: ACHARYAVAN — THE GURU UNTIES THE BLINDFOLD; YOU WALK.

lines: DO YOU KNOW ME? IT'S ME.
AN AXE HEATING IN A FIRE.
cards: At a deathbed, there's a question families ask. They lean in close, and someone says, gently: do you know me? It's me.
For a while the answer is yes, a squeeze of the hand, a name. And then, one day, it isn't.
Uddalaka's last two lessons to his son begin at that bedside, and end somewhere very different: in a courtroom, ancient style, with an axe heating in a fire.

teach.b: First, the bedside. When a man is very ill, Uddalaka says, his relatives gather and ask: do you know me? Do you know me?

teach.h: SPEECH INTO MIND, INTO BREATH, INTO BEING.
teach.b: As long as his speech hasn't gone into his mind, his mind into his breath, his breath into heat, and heat into the highest deity, he knows them. When it has, he doesn't.

It's the creation story from ten days ago, running backward: everything folds back, step by step, into Being. Then the second picture, a hard one. In the ancient world, one way to test an accused person was an ordeal.
They bring a man with his hands tied. He's taken something, they say. He's a thief.
Heat the axe for him. If he did it, he makes himself false. Covering himself with untruth, he grips the hot axe, is burned, and is killed.
If he didn't, he makes himself true.
Covered with truth, he grips the axe, is not burned, and is set free. The Upanishad isn't teaching courtroom procedure, and nobody here is recommending an ordeal.
It uses a picture its listeners knew to say one thing: a person wrapped in truth stands on what is real, and the fire can't reach him. A person wrapped in falsehood is standing on nothing.
This is satya, truthfulness, one of the oldest Hindu virtues.
The word grows from sat, Being, the very thing Uddalaka has taught all along: to be true is to stand on what is.
Another Upanishad puts it in three words, satyam eva jayate, truth alone wins, and India carries that line under its national emblem. Then, for the last time, the refrain: you are that, Shvetaketu.
And the chapter ends with one quiet line: and he understood it. After all his father's pictures, the son gets it.

how: Satya, truthfulness, is counted among the basic virtues in many Hindu ethical lists, including the yamas of the Yoga Sutras. 'Satyam eva jayate', truth alone wins (Mundaka Upanishad 3.1.6), is India's national motto, written beneath the state emblem.

o: the king who tests the accused with a hot axe
the thief brought in with his hands tied
the father who teaches Shvetaketu, you are that

games.q: what's inside the lessons — tap the pairs.
p: the first step back into Being
grips the axe and is burned
grips the axe and is set free

s: the Upanishad is teaching how courts should work
it uses an ordeal its listeners knew as a picture of truth and falsehood.
at death, speech goes into mind, mind into breath, breath into heat
and heat into the highest deity: the creation story running backward.
chapter six ends with Shvetaketu understanding
and he understood it. yes, he understood.

games.q: a friend asks why truth is more than good manners in Hinduism. what fits Uddalaka's teaching?
o: because lies get found out sooner or later.
satya grows from sat, Being: a true word stands on what's real, a lie on nothing.
because the gods burn liars, like the thief in the story.
games.why: the hot axe is a picture, not a threat. satya is standing on what is real; falsehood stands on nothing.

practice: Say quietly, three times, satyam eva jayate: truth alone wins. Then say one plain, true sentence about your day, including the part you'd usually dress up a little. Don't fix anything.
Just feel what it's like to stand on what's real.

wordCard.voice: Uddalaka, giving his last two lessons to his son. Everything folds back into Being at death, and one covered in truth is not burned.

orig.note: Sanskrit paraśu: axe. paraśuṃ tapata: heat the axe, the cry at the ordeal.

carryVoice: Your line: satya, truth stands on what is real. Tomorrow, a new teacher, and a sage in sorrow. Until then.

sources.ref: Chandogya Upanishad 6.15.1–3 (the dying man; speech into mind, mind into breath, breath into heat)
Chandogya Upanishad 6.16.1–3 (the heated axe; and he understood it)
